Three children, three continents, and I speak to one of them properly. I have stopped pretending that is an accident.
Was there something? A row, a moment, anything you could point at?
Nothing. We grew apart, which is a much harder thing to explain than a fight. There is nobody to forgive.
If I had retired five years earlier, I would be much further along with my own. That is the sentence I keep saying to myself.
And would you? Or would you have found something else to be busy with? I ask myself that one too.
Probably the second. If I were a different sort of man, I would have said something at his wedding.

My generation was taught to provide. That was the whole job, and I did it well, and nobody ever once taught us to explain anything. You did not say things out loud. You paid for the house and you were there on Sunday and that was understood to be the same as saying it. And here is the part that people expect to be dramatic and never is. There was no fight. There was never a moment I could point at and say, that is where it went. There was distance, and it took about six years to arrive, and by the time I noticed it, it had already been there for two. Now, would I do it differently? I say yes, and I say I would have said things at the time. But I am seventy and I have learned to be careful with that sentence, because I might well have found something else to be busy with. That is the honest answer and it is not a comfortable one.

Here is what goes wrong when people describe the ones they love. They reach for the largest possible words. He is a good man. She is wonderful. My father was a hard worker. Every one of those is true and not one of them can be answered, because there is nothing in it that belongs to a particular person. So use the rule you would use for a character in a film. One specific habit. One specific moment. And then what those two things tell you about them. He answers every message within a minute and he has never once asked me for anything. Now I know him, and now I can ask you something. And a note about the tenses, because this is where it gets technical. Family talk almost never sits in one time. Something happened decades ago and you are living with the result this week. English will ask you to choose which half of the sentence is in the past and which half is now, and that choice is not decoration. It is the whole meaning.

Nora tells Braulio that she has three children on three continents and speaks properly to only one of them. She says there was no argument at all, and that growing apart is harder to explain than a fight because there is nobody to forgive. Braulio says that if he had retired five years earlier he would be much further along with his own children. Nora asks whether he really would have, or whether he would have found something else to be busy with. Then she tells him that they are waiting, and that they are not going to start the conversation themselves.
